questions.stem: A 71 year old man has passed black, tarry, foul-smelling stools for 2 days. He had a drug-eluting coronary stent inserted 5 months ago and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He feels dizzy on standing. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. Abdominal examination is soft and non-tender. Rectal examination shows melaena.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of his bleeding?
questions.e: Melaena on aspirin plus clopidogrel points to an upper GI bleed, most often a peptic ulcer. Colonic bleeding usually looks red or maroon.

steps.x: **Melaena** is digested blood, so the source is proximal. Dual antiplatelets plus tachycardia = significant GI bleed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Black tarry stool on antiplatelets = upper GI bleed.

elim: Haemorrhoids give fresh red blood on the paper, not black tarry stool.
Colonic bleeding is usually red or maroon; melaena means blood digested from above.
No liver disease or alcohol history; antiplatelets cause ulcer bleeding, not varices.
Haematuria is a bleeding site on antiplatelets, but it does not cause black stools.

steps.x: **D. Upper gastrointestinal tract.** Melaena + antiplatelet = upper GI bleed until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman is brought to the emergency department with a sudden severe headache and vomiting that began 2 hours ago. She takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a recent TIA. Her GCS is 12 and she has a new left hemiparesis. Her BP is 182/98 mmHg. CT head shows a hyperdense area in the right basal ganglia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A hyperdense lesion on CT with sudden headache and focal deficit is an intracerebral haemorrhage, a major bleeding risk of antiplatelets. Early ischaemic stroke is not hyperdense.

clues: hyperdense area in the right basal ganglia
steps.x: Hyperdense on CT = **fresh blood**. Antiplatelets increase the risk of major bleeding, including intracranial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sudden headache, vomiting, focal signs and blood on CT: intracerebral haemorrhage.

elim: Not suggested: no prothrombotic history, and the CT shows a bleed in brain tissue.
Gives diffuse confusion and headache, not a focal hyperdense lesion.
An early infarct is normal or hypodense on CT, not hyperdense.
Needs a preceding seizure; there was none.

steps.x: **C. Intracerebral haemorrhage.** Major bleeds on antiplatelets: GI and intracranial.

questions.stem: An 83 year old man on aspirin 75 mg daily after a stroke is found by his carer to be pale and drowsy. He has had no vomiting and has not noticed any blood. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 86/54 mmHg. His abdomen is soft. Rectal examination is not yet done.

visual.title: Haemoglobin over the last month
visual.caption: A steady fall in Hb in a patient on aspirin suggests ongoing blood loss.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
questions.e: Unexplained hypotension and pallor on aspirin should raise immediate suspicion of a GI bleed, even before melaena is seen. Do a rectal exam and FBC.

steps.x: On an antiplatelet, **unexplained hypotension** = GI bleed until proven otherwise. Pallor suggests anaemia from blood loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Shock + pallor on aspirin: occult GI bleed.

elim: No steroid history, pigmentation or electrolyte clue; much rarer.
Pallor with tachycardia and no chest pain or heart failure signs points to blood loss.
A stroke does not cause shock; hypotension needs another cause.
Fever and urinary symptoms would be expected; pallor suggests bleeding.

steps.x: **C. Occult gastrointestinal bleeding.** Unexplained hypotension on aspirin or clopidogrel = think GI bleed.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had burning epigastric pain for 6 weeks, worse after meals, and occasional nausea. Aspirin 75 mg daily was started 2 months ago after a myocardial infarction. He has no weight loss or dysphagia. He does not drink alcohol. His Hb is 138 g/L. Epigastric tenderness is present.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: Dyspepsia starting after aspirin with epigastric tenderness is most likely aspirin-induced peptic ulcer disease, from loss of gastroprotective prostaglandins.

clues: Aspirin 75 mg daily was started 2 months ago
steps.x: Burning, meal-related epigastric pain that **began with aspirin**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aspirin GI irritation: dyspepsia or peptic ulcer.

elim: Severe pain radiating to the back with vomiting; not 6 weeks of mild meal-related pain.
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals lasting hours, not burning epigastric pain.
No red flags: no weight loss, dysphagia or anaemia.
Pain is meal-related and burning, not exertional.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin-induced peptic ulcer disease.** Aspirin side effects: dyspepsia, PUD, asthma, renal effects.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent. His GP reviews several symptoms he has noticed over the last month. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. His Hb is 141 g/L.
questions.q: Which symptom would indicate major rather than minor bleeding?
o: Prolonged bleeding from a shaving cut
questions.e: Melaena means GI bleeding, which the notes class as major bleeding alongside intracranial haemorrhage. Bruising, epistaxis and gum bleeding are minor.

steps.x: Sort bleeding into **minor** (bruising, epistaxis, gums) and **major** (GI, intracranial).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The only major bleed listed is a GI bleed, shown by black stools.

elim: Gum bleeding is minor antiplatelet bleeding.
Easy bruising is minor bleeding.
Epistaxis that stops is minor bleeding.
Prolonged bleeding from small cuts is minor.

steps.x: **A. Black stools.** Major = GI bleed or intracranial haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman with asthma and nasal polyps had a TIA 2 weeks ago. Since then she has needed her salbutamol inhaler several times a day and has had a blocked, running nose. She started five new medicines after the TIA. Her respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute and peak flow is 62% of her best. There is widespread wheeze.
questions.q: Which new medicine is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Asthma with nasal polyps is the setting for aspirin-sensitive asthma; aspirin started after a TIA explains worsening wheeze and rhinitis.

steps.x: Asthma + **nasal polyps** + new antiplatelet after TIA = aspirin exacerbating asthma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aspirin-sensitive asthma.

elim: Causes ankle oedema and flushing, not bronchospasm.
Causes myalgia, not wheeze.
Does not cause aspirin-sensitive asthma; it is the alternative when aspirin is not tolerated.
Not a cause of bronchospasm.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin.** Aspirin can exacerbate asthma, especially with nasal polyps.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman on aspirin after a myocardial infarction has had black stools for 3 days. She looks pale. Lying, her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. She has no abdominal tenderness. Her doctor wants to judge how much blood she has lost.
questions.q: Which examination finding would best indicate significant blood loss?
questions.e: Signs of significant bleeding are hypotension (including a postural drop) and pallor from anaemia. Tenderness locates the source but does not measure the loss.

clues: judge how much blood she has lost
steps.x: Signs of **significant bleeding**: hypotension and pallor. Lying BP is normal, so look for a postural drop.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A postural fall in BP.

elim: Suggests heart failure or low albumin, not acute blood loss.
Minor antiplatelet bleeding; says nothing about volume lost.
Suggests an ulcer source but not the size of the bleed.
Suggest low platelets; antiplatelets leave the count normal.

steps.x: **D. Fall in BP on standing.** Significant bleeding: hypotension, tachycardia, pallor.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a second myocardial infarction 3 months after a coronary stent. Angiography shows stent thrombosis. He has taken all his medicines: aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, ramipril and omeprazole, which his GP started for dyspepsia. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. ECG shows anterior ST elevation.
questions.q: Which of his medicines most likely contributed to the stent thrombosis?
questions.e: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which converts clopidogrel into its active metabolite, so clopidogrel works less well and the stent can thrombose.

clues: omeprazole, which his GP started for dyspepsia
steps.x: Stent thrombosis despite taking clopidogrel: look for something **blocking clopidogrel activation**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Omeprazole, via CYP2C19.

elim: Aspirin is part of the protective dual antiplatelet therapy.
Statins stabilise plaque and reduce events.
Beta-blockers are protective after MI.
ACE inhibitors are protective after MI and do not affect clopidogrel.

steps.x: **D. Omeprazole.** Omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce clopidogrel efficacy.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman is admitted with confusion, fever and purple spots on her legs. Four weeks ago she had a coronary stent and started a new antiplatelet. She also takes atorvastatin, ramipril and bisoprolol. Her temperature is 38.1°C. Blood film shows fragmented red cells.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Fever, confusion, purpura, thrombocytopenia, AKI and schistocytes after a new antiplatelet is TTP, a rare but serious complication of clopidogrel (a thienopyridine).

steps.x: Fever + confusion + purpura + low platelets + AKI + **schistocytes** = **TTP**. Which antiplatelet is a thienopyridine?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clopidogrel.

elim: Aspirin is not the antiplatelet linked to TTP; the thienopyridines are.
Statins cause myopathy, not TTP.
Not associated with TTP.
Causes cough, angioedema and hyperkalaemia, not TTP.

steps.x: **D. Clopidogrel.** Clopidogrel (thienopyridine) = rare TTP.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man bleeds for 3 hours after a dental extraction. He had an ischaemic stroke last year and takes clopidogrel 75 mg daily. He has no personal or family history of bleeding. His platelet count is 254 × 10⁹/L and INR is 1.0.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his prolonged bleeding?
questions.e: Clopidogrel inhibits platelet aggregation, so the count and INR stay normal while bleeding is prolonged.

steps.x: Normal platelet **count**, normal clotting, but on an antiplatelet: the platelets are there but do not **work**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Impaired platelet function from clopidogrel.

elim: INR is normal and he has no bleeding history.
The platelet count is normal.
Would prolong the INR.
Would give a lifelong bleeding history.

steps.x: **C. Inhibition of platelet aggregation.** Antiplatelets: normal count, impaired function.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has vomited blood twice. She takes aspirin 75 mg daily for ischaemic heart disease and ibuprofen for knee pain. She does not drink alcohol and has no liver disease. She has not been retching beforehand. After fluids her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Endoscopy is arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on endoscopy?
questions.e: Aspirin (and NSAIDs) reduce gastroprotective prostaglandins, causing peptic ulcers, the commonest cause of haematemesis on antiplatelets.

steps.x: Aspirin + NSAID = **prostaglandin loss** = ulcer. No retching, no liver disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A bleeding peptic ulcer.

elim: Rarely bleeds and is a long-term reflux change.
No weight loss, dysphagia or early satiety.
Needs forceful retching before the bleed; she had none.
Needs portal hypertension; no liver disease or alcohol.

steps.x: **E. Peptic ulcer.** Aspirin GI bleed = peptic ulcer.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man on aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent has a nosebleed that has needed packing, and bruises on both arms. He has visible blood in his urine. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of his blood results?
o: Low platelet count, normal PT and APTT
Normal platelet count, normal PT and APTT
Normal platelet count, prolonged APTT only
Normal platelet count, prolonged PT only
Prolonged PT and APTT with low fibrinogen
questions.e: Antiplatelets impair platelet function, not number or the clotting cascade, so the count, PT and APTT are typically normal.

steps.x: Bruising, epistaxis and haematuria on antiplatelets. What do antiplatelets do to the **tests**?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Everything normal: count, PT and APTT.

elim: Antiplatelets do not lower the count; that suggests ITP or TTP.
Suggests heparin or haemophilia.
Suggests warfarin or vitamin K deficiency.
Suggests DIC.

steps.x: **B. Normal platelet count, normal PT and APTT.** Antiplatelet bleeding: tests normal, function impaired.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has had coffee-ground vomiting and melaena for a day. She takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent. After 1 litre of IV fluid her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg. Her Hb is 89 g/L.
questions.q: Which investigation would both find and treat the source of bleeding?
questions.e: Endoscopy is the gold standard for a suspected GI bleed: it localises the source and allows treatment (e.g. clips, adrenaline).

steps.x: Upper GI bleed on antiplatelets. The test that **localises and treats**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper GI endoscopy.

elim: Images the small bowel but cannot treat.
Looks at the wrong end; melaena and coffee grounds are upper GI.
Cannot treat the bleeding point.
Looks for free air after perforation, not a bleed.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy.** GI bleed gold standard = endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man on clopidogrel after a stroke has passed melaena twice today. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. He feels light-headed but has no abdominal pain. A cannula is placed and IV fluids started. The registrar wants a blood test that will show how much blood he has lost.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood test to assess his blood loss?
questions.e: FBC is first-line: the Hb assesses overt or occult blood loss. Coagulation tests are usually normal on antiplatelets.

steps.x: First-line test for **blood loss** = Hb.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FBC.

elim: A marker of inflammation, not blood loss.
Usually normal on antiplatelets and does not measure loss.
Help with liver disease, not the size of the bleed.
Reflects iron stores over weeks, not an acute bleed.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count.** First-line in antiplatelet bleeding = FBC.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man is brought from a care home with a large haematoma on his thigh after a fall. His medication chart is lost; the carer knows he takes 'a blood thinner' but not which. His platelet count is 236 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.0, APTT 31 seconds (25–35).
questions.q: Which drug is he most likely taking?
questions.e: A normal coagulation profile with a bleed fits an antiplatelet, which spares the clotting cascade. Warfarin raises the INR and heparin or dabigatran prolong the APTT.

steps.x: Normal INR and APTT: the drug does **not** act on the clotting cascade.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An antiplatelet: clopidogrel.

elim: Prolongs the APTT.
A vitamin K antagonist, so the INR would be raised.
Prolongs the APTT.
Would raise the INR.

steps.x: **A. Clopidogrel.** Normal coagulation profile helps distinguish antiplatelet from anticoagulant bleeding.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has had tiredness and indigestion for 3 months. She takes aspirin 75 mg daily after a stroke. She has epigastric discomfort and no change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding. She looks pale. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Iron deficiency anaemia with dyspepsia on aspirin suggests slow upper GI blood loss from an ulcer; endoscopy is the gold standard to find and treat it.

steps.x: Low Hb and **microcytosis** = chronic blood loss. Dyspepsia on aspirin = upper GI source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper GI endoscopy.

elim: Shows structure only and cannot biopsy or treat.
No lower GI symptoms; the dyspepsia points upwards.
Not first for suspected peptic ulcer bleeding.
Confirms occult blood but does not find the source.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy.** Occult GI blood loss on aspirin: endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man started clopidogrel 3 weeks ago after a coronary stent. He now has fever, headache, intermittent confusion and petechiae on his legs. His temperature is 38.0°C. Investigations show Hb 88 g/L (130–180), platelets 19 × 10⁹/L (150–400) and creatinine 188 µmol/L (60–110).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to support the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Suspected clopidogrel-associated TTP: a blood film showing schistocytes confirms microangiopathic haemolysis quickly, while ADAMTS13 activity is sent.

steps.x: Clopidogrel + fever, confusion, low platelets, AKI, anaemia = **TTP**. Look for **fragmented red cells**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood film for schistocytes.

elim: Invasive and not needed to show microangiopathy.
May exclude a bleed but does not diagnose TTP.
Positive in autoimmune haemolysis; TTP is DAT negative.
Dangerous with platelets of 19 and not diagnostic.

steps.x: **A. Blood film.** TTP: blood film first, ADAMTS13 to confirm.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman takes aspirin 75 mg daily, started years ago 'to protect her heart'. She has never had a heart attack, stroke or stent. She has had three nosebleeds this month, each stopping with pressure, and bruises easily. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. Her Hb is 129 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: The bleeding is minor and she is stable, so after assessing severity the next step is to stop the antiplatelet, especially as there is no indication for it.

clues: has never had a heart attack, stroke or stent
steps.x: Step 1: assess severity (**minor**, stable). Step 2: **stop the antiplatelet**. Here there is no indication anyway.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop aspirin.

elim: A PPI protects the stomach, not the nose; the drug has no clear indication.
Ongoing minor bleeding with no indication for aspirin.
For life-threatening bleeding only.
There is no indication for any antiplatelet.

steps.x: **D. Stop aspirin.** Assess severity first, then stop the antiplatelet.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man on aspirin has vomited a large amount of fresh blood. On arrival his pulse rate was 128 bpm and BP 82/50 mmHg. He has received 2 litres of fluid and 2 units of blood. His pulse rate is now 98 bpm and BP 110/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: After resuscitation for a severe bleed, treat according to the source: urgent endoscopy for a GI bleed.

clues: vomited a large amount of fresh blood
received 2 litres of fluid and 2 units of blood
steps.x: Severe bleed, now **resuscitated**. Next: treat the **source**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent endoscopy.

elim: He has had a major bleed and needs urgent treatment of the source.
Used if endoscopy fails, not first.
He is still at high risk of rebleeding.
Restarting comes after the source is treated and risks are weighed.

steps.x: **E. Urgent upper GI endoscopy.** Resuscitate, then endoscopy for a GI bleed.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man had a drug-eluting coronary stent inserted 6 weeks ago and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He was admitted with a bleeding duodenal ulcer, which was treated endoscopically 2 days ago. He has had no further bleeding and his Hb is stable. He asks what will happen with his antiplatelets.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach?
o: Continue both drugs and add a platelet transfusion daily
Restart after weighing rebleeding against stent thrombosis risk
Restart only when his Hb is normal in 3 months
questions.e: Once the bleeding is controlled, the decision on when to restart balances ongoing bleeding risk against the risk of thrombosis, here very high with a recent stent.

clues: drug-eluting coronary stent inserted 6 weeks ago
steps.x: Bleeding controlled, but a **6-week-old stent** clots without antiplatelets.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A balanced decision on restarting.

elim: Not a treatment strategy.
A recent stent carries a high risk of thrombosis without antiplatelets.
Far too long without cover for a 6-week-old stent.
Warfarin does not protect a coronary stent and also causes bleeding.

steps.x: **C. Restart after weighing rebleeding against stent thrombosis risk.** Restart = bleeding risk vs thrombosis risk.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman takes clopidogrel 75 mg daily for peripheral arterial disease after an angioplasty 2 years ago. She has no coronary stent. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. She is listed for an elective total hip replacement. The surgeon asks the pre-assessment clinic when she should take her last dose.
questions.q: How long before surgery should clopidogrel be stopped?
questions.e: Clopidogrel is stopped 7 days before surgery because it irreversibly inhibits platelets, which must be replaced. Warfarin is stopped 5 days before.

steps.x: Irreversible platelet inhibition: new platelets needed. Clopidogrel interval = **7 days**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 7 days.

elim: Platelets remain inhibited for their lifespan; 1 day is far too short.
Longer than needed and leaves her unprotected.
Too short; irreversible inhibition outlasts this.
This is the warfarin interval, not clopidogrel.

steps.x: **E. 7 days.** Clopidogrel 7 days, warfarin 5 days.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with atrial fibrillation takes warfarin. His INR is stable at 2.4. He is due to have an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 3 weeks and is not at high thrombotic risk. He also takes ramipril and atorvastatin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about his warfarin?
o: Switch to aspirin 2 weeks before surgery
questions.e: Warfarin is stopped 5 days before surgery (clopidogrel is 7 days), with LMWH cover where needed.

steps.x: Perioperative warfarin: **5 days**, compare clopidogrel **7 days**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop 5 days before.

elim: Unacceptable bleeding risk during abdominal surgery.
Too short for the INR to fall.
That is the clopidogrel interval.
Aspirin does not prevent AF stroke and still bleeds.

steps.x: **C. Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery.** Warfarin 5 days before surgery.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman on warfarin for a previous DVT has had melaena for a day. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg. She is pale and has no abdominal pain. Endoscopy is planned and the team decide the bleeding needs reversal of anticoagulation. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of her anticoagulation?
o: Continue warfarin and give 1 mg oral vitamin K
Stop warfarin and give 5 mg IV vitamin K
questions.e: For bleeding on warfarin needing reversal, stop warfarin and give 5 mg IV vitamin K, then recheck the INR at 12 hours aiming for below 1.5.

steps.x: Warfarin bleed = **raised INR**. Reverse with vitamin K, IV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop warfarin, IV vitamin K 5 mg.

elim: Too little and too slow, and warfarin must stop.
Reverses heparin, not warfarin.
Does not reverse warfarin.
Her problem is a raised INR, not platelets.

steps.x: **E. Stop warfarin and give 5 mg IV vitamin K.** Warfarin reversal: stop, 5 mg IV vitamin K, INR at 12 h.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man on warfarin with a large thigh haematoma was given 5 mg IV vitamin K and his warfarin was stopped. His INR on admission was 6.2. The ward team asks when to repeat the INR and what result they are aiming for.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate plan?
o: No recheck is needed after vitamin K
Recheck at 1 hour, aiming for below 3.0
Recheck at 12 hours, aiming for 2.0 to 3.0
Recheck at 12 hours, aiming for below 1.5
Recheck in 1 week, aiming for below 1.5
questions.e: After IV vitamin K, the INR is rechecked at 12 hours to confirm it is below 1.5.

steps.x: Vitamin K works over **hours**. Target is reversal, **below 1.5**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 12 hours, below 1.5.

elim: The response must be confirmed.
Vitamin K takes hours to work, and 3.0 is still anticoagulated.
2 to 3 is the therapeutic range, not reversal.
Far too late in an acute bleed.

steps.x: **D. Recheck at 12 hours, aiming for below 1.5.** INR at 12 h, target <1.5.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is recovering from a myocardial infarction. Five years ago aspirin caused severe wheeze needing admission. He has asthma and nasal polyps and uses a steroid inhaler. His pulse rate is 74 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and his chest is clear today. The cardiology team want to start long-term antiplatelet therapy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antiplatelet for him?
questions.e: Clopidogrel is used when aspirin is not tolerated, such as aspirin-sensitive asthma.

steps.x: Aspirin **not tolerated** (aspirin-sensitive asthma). Which antiplatelet replaces it?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clopidogrel.

elim: Aspirin-sensitive asthma is not dose-safe.
Covers the symptom but keeps the trigger.
He needs antiplatelet therapy after an MI.
An anticoagulant, not the standard post-MI antiplatelet.

steps.x: **C. Clopidogrel.** Aspirin intolerance = clopidogrel.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman starts aspirin 75 mg daily after an ischaemic stroke. She has no asthma or dyspepsia. Her CT head showed an infarct and no haemorrhage. Her BP is 146/84 mmHg. A medical student asks how such a low dose prevents platelets from clumping together.
questions.q: Which mediator's synthesis does aspirin mainly reduce in platelets?
questions.e: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, preventing thromboxane A2 synthesis and so platelet aggregation.

steps.x: Aspirin blocks **COX-1** in platelets. The pro-aggregation product of COX-1 is...

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thromboxane A2.

elim: ADP acts at P2Y12, the target of clopidogrel.
Made by endothelium, not reduced by aspirin.
Endothelial; aspirin's antiplatelet effect relies on platelet thromboxane.
An adhesion protein not affected by aspirin.

steps.x: **D. Thromboxane A2.** Aspirin: COX-1 blocked, no thromboxane A2.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man takes aspirin 75 mg daily after a myocardial infarction 3 years ago. He stops it before elective surgery on his bowel. His platelet count is normal. The anaesthetist explains that a new supply of platelets is needed before his platelet function returns to normal, because the existing platelets cannot recover.
questions.q: Approximately how long does aspirin's antiplatelet effect last after the last dose?
questions.e: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and platelets have no nucleus to make more, so the effect lasts the platelet lifespan of about 7 to 10 days.

clues: a new supply of platelets is needed
steps.x: Irreversible block + no nucleus = effect lasts the **platelet lifespan**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: About 7 to 10 days.

elim: This is closer to aspirin's plasma half-life, not its effect.
Too short; the inhibition is irreversible.
Too short for platelet turnover.
Far longer than the platelet lifespan.

steps.x: **E. 7 to 10 days.** Aspirin effect = platelet lifespan, 7 to 10 days.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is started on clopidogrel and aspirin after a coronary stent. He asks why he needs two drugs if both 'thin the blood'. The pharmacist explains that clopidogrel acts on a different platelet target from aspirin.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
o: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase
Irreversible blockade of the P2Y12 ADP receptor
questions.e: Clopidogrel is a prodrug whose active metabolite irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor.

clues: a different platelet target from aspirin
steps.x: Aspirin = COX-1. Clopidogrel = **P2Y12** (ADP receptor).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Irreversible P2Y12 blockade.

elim: This is apixaban or rivaroxaban.
This is abciximab or tirofiban.
This is warfarin.
This is aspirin.

steps.x: **D. Irreversible blockade of the P2Y12 ADP receptor.** Clopidogrel: P2Y12 ADP receptor, irreversible.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has stent thrombosis 2 months after a coronary stent despite taking aspirin and clopidogrel every day. He takes no other medicines. Genetic testing shows he carries two loss-of-function alleles that make him a poor metaboliser.
questions.q: Which enzyme is most likely affected?
questions.e: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by hepatic CYP2C19; poor metabolisers make little active drug, so platelets are not inhibited.

clues: despite taking aspirin and clopidogrel every day
steps.x: Clopidogrel failure without an interacting drug: the **activating enzyme** must be weak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CYP2C19.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man on aspirin and clopidogrel has bled heavily from a skin biopsy site. His PT is 12 seconds (10–14), APTT 30 seconds (25–35) and platelet count 268 × 10⁹/L. A junior doctor is surprised the tests are normal.
questions.q: Which best explains the normal results?
o: The drugs are not being absorbed
The drugs impair platelet function, not the coagulation cascade
The drugs lower clotting factor levels below detection
The drugs only work in the arteries
The tests were taken too soon after the bleed
questions.e: PT and APTT test the clotting cascade, and the platelet count measures number; antiplatelets impair platelet function, so all stay normal despite real bleeding risk.

steps.x: PT/APTT = **cascade**. Platelet count = **number**. Antiplatelets hit **function**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Platelet function is impaired; the cascade is untouched.

elim: He is clearly bleeding, so the drugs are working.
Antiplatelets do not affect clotting factors.
Platelet inhibition is systemic.
Timing does not change PT or APTT on antiplatelets.

steps.x: **B. The drugs impair platelet function, not the coagulation cascade.** Normal PT/APTT/INR despite antiplatelet bleeding.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman develops thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura 4 weeks after starting clopidogrel. She has fever, confusion, petechiae, anaemia with schistocytes and acute kidney injury. Her platelet count is 16 × 10⁹/L, with a normal PT and APTT. A haematologist explains the likely mechanism to the team.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Clopidogrel-associated TTP is thought to relate to reduced ADAMTS13, leaving large von Willebrand multimers that form microvascular platelet thrombi.

steps.x: TTP = microvascular platelet thrombi. The enzyme missing in TTP is...

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ADAMTS13 deficiency.

elim: This is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
This is DIC, with prolonged PT and APTT.
This is HUS after E. coli O157 diarrhoea.
Causes a raised INR, not microangiopathy.

steps.x: **C. Deficiency of ADAMTS13 activity.** Thienopyridine TTP = ADAMTS13 deficiency.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man develops a gastric ulcer 3 months after starting aspirin for ischaemic heart disease. He takes no NSAIDs and is negative for Helicobacter pylori. He had 4 weeks of burning epigastric pain before a small haematemesis. His Hb is 121 g/L. He asks why a heart tablet harmed his stomach.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Reduced platelet count in the gastric mucosa
questions.e: COX-1 inhibition also reduces prostaglandins that protect the stomach (mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow), explaining dyspepsia and peptic ulcers.

steps.x: Aspirin blocks COX-1 everywhere, including the stomach, where COX-1 makes **protective prostaglandins**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Loss of gastroprotective prostaglandins.

elim: That is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
This reduces acid; it is how omeprazole works.
Aspirin does not lower the platelet count.
Aspirin does not act on P2Y12, and stimulation would not cause ulcers.

steps.x: **C. Reduced gastroprotective prostaglandins.** Aspirin ulcers: COX-1 inhibition reduces gastric prostaglandins.
